newsitem.title: USA: GM parts strike in Ohio threatens broad shutdown.
newsitem.headline: GM parts strike in Ohio threatens broad shutdown.

text.p: The third strike to hit General Motors Corp. in about five weeks threatened on Tuesday to force a broad shutdown of GM's North American vehicle operations and affect other automakers that buy GM electrical components.
In Warren, Ohio, about 8,200 members of the International Union of Electronic workers walked off the job at 18 plants operated by GM's Delphi Packard Electric Systems division just after midnight.

The plants produce vehicle wiring harness components and other electrical parts for nearly all of GM's North American-built cars and trucks. The harnesses are used to distribute electrical power and signals throughout a vehicle.

Analysts estimate that GM could begin shutting down factories by late next week. Much of the assembly work for the harnesses is done in Mexico, so GM likely has more inventory in transit, but not immediately available for its factories.

In March 1996, a 17-day strike against two GM brake plants in Dayton, Ohio, forced GM to idle 26 of 29 North American assembly plants. The walkout idled more than 150,000 workers and slashed GM profits by $900 million.

The issues keeping IUE Local 717 and GM from reaching a new local labour agreement, like ongoing assembly plant strikes in Oklahoma City and Pontiac, Mich., involve job security. The union, among other things, has demanded that GM guarantee that it will not unilaterally move more jobs to Mexico.
"We're trying to keep all of our people working so they have a place to retire from," Local 717 President Nick Border said.
Negotiations to resolve the dispute resumed Tuesday afternoon about 13 hours after the strike began.

In a statement, Delphi Packard Electric said it is "extremely disappointed" by the walkout. "Our main focus is on the impact this strike will have on our customers, both General Motors and non-GM. Any interruption either actual or potential, in the chain of supply to our customers poses a great risk to the retention and ongoing expansion of our business," the GM unit said.
GM lists about 34 other car and truck makers worldwide as customers of Delphi Packard Electric, but not all of them use components from the Ohio plants.

Other demands by the union include abolishing the bottom tier of the plants' three-tier wage scale. Bottom-tier workers make 55 percent of the top-tier full wage. Local 717 members rejected a tentative pact in March, in part because it did not alter the tiered-wage scale.

GM has been hit with a rash of strikes in the past year over local labour contracts at individual plants, but this marks the first time in years that the automaker has simultaneously battled three major strikes involving two different unions.
GM shares fell $1.375 to $56.875 on the New York Stock Exchange, but analysts attributed the drop more to a downgrade of the stock by PaineWebber Inc. than to the strike.

PaineWebber auto analyst Michael Ward said in a research report that he cut his rating on GM stock to neutral from attractive in part because GM's second-quarter operating profits from North America are likely to fall from the first quarter, largely due to the strikes and excessive dealer inventory levels.

"GM's earnings continue to suffer from labour unrest, and it's our fear that at some point the market will become less forgiving," Ward wrote, adding that near-term news about GM is likely to be more negative than positive.

With about 25 GM plants still lacking local labour agreements and several union locals requesting permission to strike, Schroder Wertheim analyst John Casesa said he expects GM's labour woes to continue.
"This is part of a continuing process of resizing this company," he said Tuesday. "Until GM's costs are matched with the market there's going to continue to be this tension."
Workers represented by the United Auto Workers union struck GM's Oklahoma City car plant on April 4, while UAW members walked off the job at the company's Pontiac, Mich., truck plant on April 22.

The Pontiac plant is one of three North American factories that produce GM's full-size Chevrolet and GMC pickup trucks. The Oklahoma City plant builds the Chevrolet Malibu and Oldsmobile Cutlass mid-size sedans.
